summary: The note describes the East African Rift (EAR), an active continental rift zone where the African Plate is splitting into the Somali and Nubian plates at 6–7 mm per year. It covers the rift's extent and branches, competing theories of its evolution (mantle plumes, superplume, and the 2009 magmatism-tectonics feedback view), its volcanoes and seismicity, its effects on regional climate, and its role in discoveries of hominid fossils.
one_line: Overview of the East African Rift, an active continental rift in East Africa covering its structure, evolution theories, volcanism, climate effects and human-fossil significance.
key_facts: The East African Rift began developing around the onset of the Miocene, 22–25 million years ago.
The African Plate is splitting into the Somali Plate and the Nubian Plate at a rate of 6–7 mm (0.24–0.28 in) per year.
The rift system consists of three microplates: the Victoria Microplate to the north, and the Rovuma and Lwandle microplates to the south.
The Davie Ridge is a 2,200 km-long (1,400 mi) relic fracture zone that cuts across the West Somali basin.
In 1972 it was proposed that the EAR was caused by differences in crustal density rather than tectonic activity.
The most recent and accepted view, put forth in 2009, holds that magmatism and plate tectonics have a feedback with one another, controlled by oblique rifting conditions.
According to marine geologist Kathleen Crane, the rift could eventually cause eastern Africa to separate from the mainland, although this could take tens of millions of years.
The EAR is the largest seismically active rift system on Earth today.
Seismic events in the past century are estimated to have reached a maximum moment magnitude of 7.0.
Ol Doinyo Lengai is currently the only active natrocarbonatite volcano on Earth.
The 2008 eruption of Dalafilla is the largest recorded eruption in Ethiopian history.
Erta Ale is a basaltic shield volcano in the Afar Region of northeastern Ethiopia, active continuously since at least 1967.
The Somali Jet is responsible for roughly half the global cross-equatorial atmospheric mass flux in the lower branch of the Hadley Circulation.
'Lucy', a partial australopithecine skeleton discovered by anthropologist Donald Johanson, dates back over 3 million years.
In 2008, Chororapithecus abyssinicus, a 10-million-year-old ape, was found in the Afar rift in eastern Ethiopia.
